# [Quasi-Majorana]{.nowrap} false positives {.part data-num="01" data-kicker="01 · Partial-shell nanowires" data-sub="Majorana zero modes, and the trivial zero modes that impersonate them"}

![](assets/figs/s04_rs_partial_qmajo.svg){.part-art}

::: {.notes}
(0:05) Part one: the Majorana nanowire and its most common impostor.
:::

## A nanowire turns topological above a critical Zeeman field

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="44%"}
Rashba nanowire, proximitized, in a Zeeman field:

::: {.eq}
$$
H = \Bigl[\tfrac{p_z^2}{2m^*} - \mu\Bigr]\tau_z + \alpha\, p_z \sigma_y \tau_z + V_\mathrm{Z}\,\sigma_z + \Delta\,\tau_x
$$
:::

::: {.fragment .qm-step}
- Gap at $k_z = 0$ closes at $V_\mathrm{Z}^\mathrm{c} = \sqrt{\Delta^2 + \mu^2}$
:::
::: {.fragment .qm-step}
- Reopens inverted: $Q = \operatorname{sign}\mathrm{Pf} = -1$, a Majorana zero mode (MZM) at each end
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.key}
**Class D**: the Majoranas rely on particle–hole symmetry alone ($\mathcal{P}^2 = +1$,
$\mathbb{Z}_2$ index). $\mathcal{P}$ is exact in any BdG Hamiltonian, so it survives disorder,
and all subbands share it.
:::

[With an effective time reversal $\mathcal{T}$ ($\mathcal{T}^2 = +1$, $H$ real), exact only in this ideal 1D model, the class is BDI with a $\mathbb{Z}$ index. Disorder, several subbands or a tilted field break $\mathcal{T}$: D, $\mathbb{Z}_2$.]{.symnote}
:::
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
::: {.qm-widget data-widget="olbands" style="width:810px;height:560px"}
:::
:::
::::

::: {.refs}
R. M. Lutchyn *et al.* PRL **105**, 077001 (2010) · Y. Oreg *et al.* PRL **105**, 177002 (2010) · A. Kitaev, Phys. Usp. **44**, 131 (2001)
:::

::: {.notes}
(1:20) The Majorana nanowire you have seen this week: a Rashba semiconductor,
proximitized, under a Zeeman field (paper's partial-shell parameters, constant Δ here).
[click] As V_Z grows, the gap at k = 0 closes at V_Z^c = √(Δ² + μ²). [click] Beyond it,
it reopens inverted: the Pfaffian index flips sign and a Majorana sits at each end. The
inset is the phase diagram, the dot is our wire at μ_bulk. [click] I want to insist on the
symmetry: all we need is particle–hole symmetry, which is built into the BdG formalism, so
no disorder can remove it: class D, a single Hamiltonian that all subbands share. Keep this
in mind: it is what changes in full shells. The small print: this ideal 1D Hamiltonian is
real, an effective time reversal with square +1, so strictly it is BDI with an integer
index. Disorder, several subbands or a field along the spin–orbit axis break it; only the parity
survives: class D. Nothing in this talk relies on it. Drag the slider for questions.
(If asked: −iσ_y is real, so α p_z σ_y is real; 𝒯 = K. Physically, T times a mirror.)
:::

## A Majorana shows up as a zero-bias peak at the end of the wire

:::: {.columns .v-center}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- A normal probe tunnels into the end: $dI/dV \propto$ local DOS at $z = 0$
- Abrupt end: the bulk gap closes at $V_\mathrm{Z}^\mathrm{c}$ and a zero-bias peak (ZBP)
  follows

::: {.fragment}
::: {.key .plain}
A ZBP is **necessary but not sufficient**: trivial states can also stick to zero energy
:::
:::
:::
::: {.column width="56%"}
::: {.qm-widget data-widget="ldos-vb" data-chis="1" data-w="780" style="width:820px;height:520px"}
:::
:::
::::

::: {.refs}
V. Mourik *et al.* Science **336**, 1003 (2012) · E. Prada *et al.* Nat. Rev. Phys. **2**, 575 (2020)
:::

::: {.notes}
(0:40) What the tunnel probe sees is the local density of states at the end. With an
abrupt end, the bulk gap closes at V_Z^c and a zero-bias peak appears after it: the
textbook signature (paper's partial-shell wire with an abrupt end, illustrative). [click] But
a zero-bias peak alone is not proof.
:::

## A smooth end makes the wire topological only locally

[The tunnel gate depletes the end; the potential heals over a length $\chi$: $\;\mu(z) = \mu_\mathrm{bulk}\bigl(1 - e^{-z/\chi}\bigr)$, topological wherever $V_\mathrm{Z} > \sqrt{\Delta^2 + \mu(z)^2}$]{.lead}

::: {.qm-widget data-widget="path" data-shell="partial" style="width:1440px;height:540px"}
:::

[]{.fragment .qm-step}
[]{.fragment .qm-step}

::: {.refs}
E. Prada *et al.* PRB **86**, 180503(R) (2012) · G. Kells *et al.* PRB **86**, 100503(R) (2012) · **C. Payá** *et al.* PRL **137**, 096606 (2026)
:::

::: {.notes}
(1:15) In a real device the tunnel gate depletes the end of the wire and the potential
heals smoothly over a length χ. Each point of the wire sits somewhere in the phase
diagram, so walking into the wire traces a vertical path: μ(z) goes from below zero
(insulating) up to μ_bulk. [click] Above V_Z^c, at V_Z^(1), the path goes straight from
insulating into topological: the whole wire is topological and the MZM sits at its end
(navy, it oscillates with k_F). [click] Below V_Z^c, at V_Z^(2), the path enters the
topological wedge and leaves it again at μ(z) ≈ 0.84 μ_bulk: only an island of length
≈ 1.9χ is topological. The island has two boundaries, and each hosts a Majorana
component. (Hover over the wire to see where each point sits in the diagram.)
:::

## Smooth ends pin the island's two Majoranas to zero

[$\Psi_\mathrm{L}$ and $\Psi_\mathrm{R}$ still overlap, but a smooth end cannot couple their different oscillations]{.lead}

::: {.qm-widget data-widget="qmzm" style="width:1440px;height:470px"}
:::

[]{.fragment .qm-step}

::: {.refs}
G. Kells *et al.* PRB **86**, 100503(R) (2012) · A. Vuik *et al.* SciPost Phys. **7**, 061 (2019) · F. Peñaranda *et al.* PRB **98**, 235406 (2018)
:::

::: {.notes}
(1:30) Here is that pair for the paper's wire at V_Z^(2), for many χ. Left, the two Majoranas
themselves, signed, over the shaded region where each lives. Ψ_L, at the hard end, oscillates
with the Fermi wavelength, about 120 nm. Ψ_R, at the soft edge of the island, is a smooth
bump. At χ = 50 nm they overlap strongly and the pair is split (bottom right, black).
[click] Now make the end smoother. Watch the shaded regions: they keep overlapping. The
overlap (dashed) drops by less than a decade, while the splitting falls by four: below
10⁻² Δ0 at χ ≈ 130 nm, about 10⁻⁵ at 400 nm. Distance is not what pins the pair. What
changes is the oscillation: top right, the momentum content. Ψ_L stays at k_F; Ψ_R
collapses to k ≈ 0, and its weight at k_F (the dot) falls by seven decades, in step with the
splitting. A smooth end cannot supply that momentum, nor flip the spin that comes with it,
so it cannot couple the two halves (Kells et al.; Vuik et al.: nearly opposite spins). Two
Majoranas at zero energy, close together, but nothing topological: a quasi-Majorana pair.
(If asked: here they are about one to three decay lengths of Ψ_L apart, the "partially
separated" case of Vuik et al.; separation alone would give about one decade, not four.
Illustrative sweep with the paper's routine; largest spinor component shown. Press play or
drag the slider for questions.)
:::

::: {.refs}
A. Vuik *et al.* SciPost Phys. **7**, 061 (2019) · C.-X. Liu *et al.* PRB **96**, 075161 (2017) · **C. Payá** *et al.* PRL **137**, 096606 (2026)
:::

::: {.notes}
(1:00) What the probe actually sees as the end gets smoother: χ = 1, 50, 100 and the
published 200 nm. [click ×3] The zero-bias peak creeps into the trivial phase, from
≈ 0.7 V_Z^c for χ = 200 nm. Right, paper Fig. 2: the same end LDOS versus smoothness at the
two fields marked on the left (the white line is the χ on the left). The true MZM (V_Z^(1))
gives a ZBP for any χ; the quasi-MZM (V_Z^(2)) is split for sharp ends and pins to zero
above 100–200 nm. [click] Same peak, no topology. Quasi-MZMs also reproduce quantized
peaks and 4π Josephson effects (Vuik et al.). [click] So: can a different geometry defuse
this?
:::

# Full-shell nanowires through the lens of symmetry {.part data-num="02" data-kicker="02 · Full-shell nanowires" data-sub="Two symmetry classes coexist, and the trivial one fills first"}

![](assets/img/device_full_cut.png){.part-art}

::: {.notes}
(0:05) Part two: full-shell nanowires, from the point of view of symmetry.
:::

## In a full shell, topology is driven by the magnetic flux

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
![](assets/img/device_full_cut.png){width="100%"}

::: {.small}
- An axial field threads a flux $\Phi = \pi R^2 B$ through the shell
- The pairing $\Delta\, e^{in\varphi}$ winds $n = \lfloor \Phi/\Phi_0 \rceil$ times, and a supercurrent $I_\mathrm{s} \propto n - \Phi/\Phi_0$ circulates in the shell: **Little–Parks lobes**
- Topology driven by the flux (orbital effect + radial SOC) at $B \approx 0.1$ T, only in **odd lobes**
:::
:::
::: {.column width="64%"}
::: {.qm-widget data-widget="lp" style="width:960px;height:440px"}
:::

[]{.fragment .qm-step}
[]{.fragment .qm-step}
[]{.fragment .qm-step}
[]{.fragment .qm-step}

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
[Zero-bias peaks were seen in the first lobe (Vaitiekėnas *et al.* 2020), but other mechanisms also produce them]{.small .ink2}
:::
:::
::::

::: {.refs}
S. Vaitiekėnas *et al.* Science **367**, eaav3392 (2020) · **C. Payá** *et al.* PRB **109**, 115428 (2024) · M. Valentini *et al.* Science **373**, 82 (2021)
:::

::: {.notes}
(1:00) The alternative: full-shell nanowires, where the superconductor wraps the whole core.
An axial field threads a flux, and the shell's order parameter winds n times around the
wire, n the fluxoid: the arrows turn n times going once around. [click] Lobe zero: as the
flux grows with n = 0, the mismatch between flux and winding drives a supercurrent around
the shell (the spinning arrows), I_s ∝ n − Φ/Φ0. It costs kinetic energy and shrinks the
shell gap. [click] Lobe one: at half-integer flux one more winding is cheaper, n jumps to
one, the gap reopens and the current reverses; it vanishes at Φ0 and grows again.
[click] Lobe two: same story, n = 2. These are the Little–Parks lobes. [click] The topological transition is driven by the flux, through the orbital
effect and the radial spin–orbit coupling, at fields of 0.1 T, and only in odd lobes.
Vaitiekėnas and coworkers saw zero-bias peaks in the first lobe in 2020; their origin is
debated.
:::

## The Hamiltonian splits into angular-momentum sectors

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.eq}
$$
[H, J_z] = 0, \qquad J_z = -i\partial_\varphi + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma_z + \tfrac{1}{2}n\,\tau_z
$$
:::

[$H = \bigoplus_{m_J} H_{m_J}$, one 2D problem in $(r, z)$ per sector, with]{.small}

::: {.eq}
$$
m_J = m_l + \tfrac{1}{2}(\sigma + n\tau) \;\in\; \mathbb{Z} + \tfrac{1 + n}{2}
$$
:::

[($m_l \in \mathbb{Z}$, $\sigma, \tau = \pm 1$): **$m_J = 0$ only for odd $n$**: odd lobes]{.small}

::: {.fragment .qm-step}
[Particle–hole symmetry pairs **different** sectors: $\;\mathcal{P}\,H_{m_J}\,\mathcal{P}^{-1} = -H_{-m_J}$]{.small}
:::

::: {.fragment .qm-step}
::: {.symtable}
|   | $\mathcal{P}$ inside the sector | with $\mathcal{T}$ | $\mathcal{T}$ broken |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| $m_J \neq 0$ | no: maps to $-m_J$ | [AI]{.chip} none | [A]{.chip .ink} none: trivial |
| $m_J = 0$ | yes: self-conjugate | [BDI]{.chip} $\mathbb{Z}$ | [D]{.chip .red} $\mathbb{Z}_2$: Majoranas |

: {tbl-colwidths="[15,33,20,32]"}

[$\mathcal{T}$ = time reversal × mirror through the axis, $\mathcal{T}^2 = +1$: the field breaks each but not the product. Exact in the ideal cylinder, broken by disorder.]{.symnote}
:::
:::
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.qm-widget data-widget="blocks" style="width:680px;height:420px"}
:::
:::
::::

::: {.refs}
P. San-Jose, **C. Payá** *et al.* PRB **107**, 155423 (2023) · **C. Payá** *et al.* PRB **109**, 115428 (2024) · A. Altland and M. Zirnbauer, PRB **55**, 1142 (1997)
:::

::: {.notes}
(1:15) In the cylindrical approximation the generalized angular momentum J_z — orbital,
spin and the winding of the pairing — is conserved, so H splits into independent sectors,
one per m_J. Its eigenvalues are m_l + (σ + nτ)/2: an integer only when the fluxoid n is
odd. So the sector m_J = 0 exists only in odd lobes: that is why Majoranas need odd lobes.
[click] Particle–hole symmetry, the one we rely on, maps m_J to −m_J: it pairs different
sectors. [click] So a sector with m_J ≠ 0 has no particle–hole symmetry of its own: no
topological index in 1D. These sectors only host trivial Andreev states, the CdGM analogs.
Only the self-conjugate sector m_J = 0 keeps 𝒫, and it is the only one that can host
Majoranas. Two columns, because the ideal cylinder has one more symmetry: an effective time
reversal, a mirror through the axis combined with time reversal. The field flips under each
of them, not under the product, so it survives and squares to +1. With it, the sectors are
AI and BDI; without it, once disorder breaks the mirror, A and D. Nothing changes for us:
m_J ≠ 0 has no index either way, and of BDI's integer only the parity survives, the ℤ₂ of
class D, like a partial-shell wire. From now on I just say A and D. Contrast with the
partial shell, where one class-D Hamiltonian holds all the subbands.
(If asked: in the sector basis 𝒯 is just complex conjugation, every block is real;
(T·M)² = T²M² = (−1)(−1) = +1, hence AI and not AII. It also keeps m_J, unlike the true T.)
:::

## The trivial sectors are Andreev states of a synthetic vortex

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.cartoons}
![](assets/figs/s08_cartoon_vortex.svg)

![](assets/figs/s08_cartoon_fullshell.svg){.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
:::

::: {.small}
- Abrikosov vortex: Andreev reflection off the pairing wall confines Caroli–de Gennes–Matricon states, $\delta E \sim \Delta^2/E_F$

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
- Full shell, a synthetic vortex: the winding shell confines Andreev subbands in the core, **one per $m_J$**, with $\delta E \sim \Delta$: resolvable
:::
:::
:::
::: {.column width="58%" .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
::: {.expth-row}
::: {.stack}
![](assets/figs/s09_exp.svg)
![](assets/figs/s09_theory.svg)
:::

![](assets/figs/s09_cbar.svg){.expth-cbar}
:::

[Lobe 0: hard gap. Lobes 1, 2: subgap states that disperse and skew with flux, one per $m_J$ subband]{.figcap}
:::
::::

::: {.refs}
C. Caroli, P. G. de Gennes, J. Matricon, Phys. Lett. **9**, 307 (1964) · P. San-Jose, **C. Payá** *et al.* PRB **107**, 155423 (2023) · M. T. Deng, **C. Payá** *et al.* PRL **134**, 206302 (2025)
:::

::: {.notes}
(1:00) What are those trivial sectors? A phase winding around a normal region is a vortex.
In an Abrikosov vortex, Andreev reflection off the pairing wall confines the CdGM states,
with tiny spacings Δ²/E_F. [click] The full shell is a synthetic vortex whose core is the
semiconductor: Andreev reflection at the core–shell interface confines subbands, one per
m_J, with spacings comparable to the gap. And we see them: tunneling spectroscopy on InAs/Al
full-shell wires from Copenhagen (left) and our model (right). Lobe 0 has a hard gap,
lobes 1 and 2 are full of discrete subgap states that disperse and skew with flux.
:::

## Two symmetry classes share zero energy

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="36%"}
::: {.fragment .qm-step}
- $m_J \neq 0$ (class A): CdGM analogs fill every lobe with trivial subgap states
:::
::: {.fragment .qm-step}
- $m_J = 0$ (class D): the only sector that can host an MZM, and only in odd lobes
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.key}
The Majorana coexists with trivial CdGM analogs at zero energy: the topological phase is
generically **gapless**
:::
:::
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}
::: {.qm-widget data-widget="sectors" style="width:920px;height:560px"}
:::
:::
::::

::: {.refs}
**C. Payá** *et al.* PRB **109**, 115428 (2024) · F. Peñaranda *et al.* PRR **2**, 023171 (2020)
:::

::: {.notes}
(1:00) The DOS of our device (paper Fig. 1g): Little–Parks lobes filled with CdGM analogs.
[click] Split it by sector: in grey-blue the m_J ≠ 0 sectors, class A, which fill every
lobe. [click] In red the m_J = 0 sector, class D: it exists only in the odd lobe, and
that is where the Majorana lives. [click] So the Majorana has to share zero energy with
trivial CdGM analogs of other sectors: two symmetry classes coexist, and the topological
phase is gapless.
:::

## The trivial sectors fill first: topology needs $\mu > \mu^\mathrm{ts}$

::: {.qm-widget data-widget="filling" style="width:1440px;height:600px"}
:::

[]{.fragment .qm-step}
[]{.fragment .qm-step}

::: {.refs}
**C. Payá** *et al.* PRL **137**, 096606 (2026)
:::

::: {.notes}
(1:30) This is the key difference, and it comes from that coexistence. Fill the bands, as
happens when walking into the wire from its depleted end. [click] Partial shell (left):
all subbands belong to the same class-D Hamiltonian, so whichever fills first can turn
topological right above depletion: the ordering of the bands is irrelevant. Full shell
(right): normal-state angular subbands at k_z = 0 versus m_L. The radial spin–orbit
coupling shifts the parabolas, so the band bottom is not at the m_J = 0 pair (red): the
class-A CdGM sectors are populated first, and they are trivial. [click] Topology needs
μ above the threshold μ^ts, where the class-D m_J = 0 pair fills. Along the wire (bottom strip), the
stretch where μ(z) < μ^ts is trivial: the trivial skin. (In our wire the threshold comes
from the second radial mode, ≈ 22 meV, because the first one needs unrealistic SOC.)
:::

# Smooth confinement in full shells {.part data-num="03" data-kicker="03 · Smooth confinement in full shells" data-sub="The length that creates quasi-Majoranas also hides them"}

![](assets/figs/s13_rs_full_qmajo.svg){.part-art}

::: {.notes}
(0:05) Part three: now we bring back the smooth end, in the full shell.
:::

## In a grounded shell the gate potential still heals over a length $\chi$

[Gate potential in the core: $\nabla^2\phi_g = 0$, $\;\phi_g = 0$ on the grounded shell, $\;e\phi_g = \mu_\mathrm{bulk}$ at the depleted end]{.lead}

::: {.eq .center-x}
$$
e\phi_g(r, z) = \mu_\mathrm{bulk} \sum_{\nu = 1}^{\infty}\frac{2}{k_\nu J_1(k_\nu)}\, J_0\!\Bigl(k_\nu \frac{r}{R}\Bigr)\, e^{-k_\nu z / k_1 \chi}
$$
:::

::: {.qm-widget data-widget="potential" data-h="330" style="width:1380px;height:330px"}
:::

::: {.key .plain}
**$\chi$ is a free parameter.** Unscreened, the slowest mode gives $\chi = R/k_1 \approx 29$ nm; screening by the charge that $\phi_g$ displaces needs Schrödinger–Poisson, so we absorb it into $\chi$, as in partial shells
:::

::: {.refs}
**C. Payá** *et al.* PRL **137**, 096606 (2026)
:::

::: {.notes}
(0:45) The same smooth confinement in a full shell. The charge in the core accumulates at
the shell, which we describe with a fixed dome-shaped potential U(r), plus the gate's φ_g;
μ_bulk = U(R) deep in the wire. The tunnel gate adds a correction φ_g: the grounded shell screens it, so it only
enters through the uncovered end. Inside, φ_g solves Laplace's equation (the charge is
already in U), vanishes at the shell and depletes the end: a sum of evanescent Bessel modes.
The slowest decays over χ = R/k_1, about 29 nm for our wire. What we leave out is the
screening of φ_g by the charge it displaces, which would need a self-consistent
Schrödinger–Poisson calculation. We absorb it into χ, which becomes the free smoothness
parameter, as in partial shells. Projected on the mode that can turn topological, μ(z)
heals like the partial-shell profile (right): χ plays the same role in both geometries.
:::

## $\mu(z)$ must cross a trivial skin before turning topological

[Same construction as in partial shells, now in flux within lobe 1]{.lead}

::: {.qm-widget data-widget="path" data-shell="full" style="width:1440px;height:540px"}
:::

[]{.fragment .qm-step}
[]{.fragment .qm-step}

[Inverted in flux: MZM below $\Phi^\mathrm{c}$, quasi-MZM above (the effective Zeeman energy falls with $\Phi$ within a lobe)]{.small .ink2}

::: {.refs}
**C. Payá** *et al.* PRL **137**, 096606 (2026)
:::

::: {.notes}
(1:15) Again μ(z) traces a vertical path, now in the flux–μ phase diagram of lobe 1
(schematic μ axis: the topological window μ^ts → μ_bulk is only 3 % wide). [click] MZM
case, Φ^(1): the path does not enter the topological region directly; it first crosses
the trivial region below μ^ts: the trivial skin, ≈ 3.4χ wide. The MZM sits behind it.
[click] Quasi-MZM case, Φ^(2): skin up to 3.5χ, a topological segment up to 7χ, and the
two quasi-MZMs form at its edges. Note the inversion, written below the figure: here the
MZM is at the lower flux and the quasi-MZM at the higher one (backup slide).
:::

## Quasi-Majoranas still form in full shells, but deep inside the wire

::: {.qm-widget data-widget="fs-maps" style="width:1440px;height:540px"}
:::

[]{.fragment .qm-step}
[]{.fragment .qm-step}
[]{.fragment .qm-step}
[]{.fragment .qm-step}

::: {.fragment}
::: {.key .green}
The quasi-MZM forms and pins to zero, but behind the skin: the probe at the end sees nothing
:::
:::

::: {.refs}
**C. Payá** *et al.* PRL **137**, 096606 (2026)
:::

::: {.notes}
(1:30) The same progression as for the partial shell, now in the full shell, with two views
of the m_J = 0 sector versus flux in lobe 1: left, the end LDOS, what a tunnel probe sees;
right, the DOS where μ(z) varies, what is inside the wire. χ = 5 nm, a sharp end: both agree,
the MZM below Φ^c and the gap reopening above it. [click] χ = 20 nm: inside, nothing has
changed; at the end, the peak is already about 80 times weaker. The trivial skin, ≈ 3.5χ
wide, now separates the probe from the topological segment. [click] χ = 200 nm: the end is
dark. Inside, above Φ^c, the lowest pair starts at zero and splits right away. [click]
χ = 500 nm: the pair now stays at zero over a stretch of flux above Φ^c before it splits:
the quasi-MZM is growing. [click] χ = 1 µm, paper Fig. 1h: the MZM below Φ^c and the
quasi-MZM pinned to zero up to Φ ≈ Φ0, with an exponentially small splitting; at the end,
nothing at any flux. [click] Quasi-Majoranas do form in full shells, but behind the skin,
where the probe cannot see them. (Illustrative maps with the paper's wire and routines on
the grid of Fig. 1h; the 1 µm DOS is Fig. 1h itself; one colour scale per column.)
:::

## The probe sees no quasi-Majorana: no false positives in full shells

::: {.qm-widget data-widget="ldos-chi" data-rows="partial,full" style="width:1400px;height:560px"}
![](assets/img/device_partial.png){.qm-asset data-key="device_partial"}
![](assets/img/device_full.png){.qm-asset data-key="device_full"}
:::

[]{.fragment .qm-step}
[]{.fragment .qm-step}
[]{.fragment .qm-step}

::: {.refs}
**C. Payá** *et al.* PRL **137**, 096606 (2026)
:::

::: {.notes}
(1:30) The key result: end LDOS versus smoothness. Partial shell, as before: the MZM gives a
ZBP for any χ and the quasi-MZM pins to zero for smooth ends: a false positive. [click]
Full shell, true MZM: visible for sharp ends, but the skin grows with χ and the end signal
is gone beyond ≈ 19 nm. Quasi-MZM: split states for very sharp ends, and then nothing.
[click] So: sharp end, the probe works; smooth end, the trivial skin hides everything.
No false positive. [click] And the quasi-MZM is there: dashed, its energy from the
m_J = 0 DOS, once it leaves the gap edge. It pins to zero exactly where the end LDOS is dark.
:::

## One length scale both pins the impostor and buries it

::: {.qm-widget data-widget="window" style="width:1400px;height:560px"}
:::

[]{.fragment .qm-step}
[]{.fragment .qm-step}

::: {.figcap .center-x}
Visible: end LDOS above 1 % of its maximum · Energy: end-LDOS splitting and closed-wire pole (partial), $m_J = 0$ DOS peak (full, this talk)
:::

::: {.refs}
**C. Payá** *et al.* PRL **137**, 096606 (2026)
:::

::: {.notes}
(1:00) Why can't we escape this? Pinning a quasi-MZM needs a smooth end: smooth on the
scale of the Majorana length, so that it cannot couple the two halves of the pair. Partial shell: pinned from χ ≈ 130 nm, and it stays visible at
the end for every χ: the two windows overlap, and that overlap is the false positive.
[click] Full shell: the same χ also sets the width of the trivial skin, ≈ 3.5χ. Visibility
dies at ≈ 19 nm. The hidden pair leaves the gap edge (dotted) at ≈ 35 nm and is pinned
below 10⁻² Δ0 from ≈ 55 nm, three times later; by 350 nm it is below 10⁻³ Δ0. (If asked: at
Φ^(2) the minigap itself is only ≈ 1.2·10⁻² Δ0, so the pair is born pinned; any threshold
gives the same ordering.)
[click] There is no window where it is both pinned and visible: the scale that produces
the skin is the scale that controls what the probe sees. Quasi-Majoranas cannot be false
positives in full shells.
:::

## Conclusions {.no-kicker}

::: {.ccards}
::: {.ccard}
![](assets/figs/s16_thumb_partial.svg)

#### Partial shells

Smooth ends create quasi-MZMs that the probe cannot tell from MZMs
:::

::: {.ccard .fragment .fade-up}
![](assets/figs/s16_thumb_skin.svg)

#### Full shells

Trivial sectors fill first: $\mu(z)$ crosses a trivial skin $\approx 3.5\chi$ wide
:::

::: {.ccard .fragment .fade-up}
![](assets/figs/s16_thumb_full.svg)

#### No false positives

The same $\chi$ that pins the impostor buries it behind the skin
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.key .mt-3}
A zero-bias peak at the end of a full-shell wire is not a quasi-Majorana. No peak? The skin
may hide a true MZM: sharp barriers give the most informative measurements.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
(1:00) To conclude. In partial shells, smooth confinement creates quasi-Majoranas that local
spectroscopy cannot tell from MZMs. [click] Full shells are synthetic vortices: the trivial
CdGM sectors coexist with the m_J = 0 sector and fill first, so μ(z) has to cross a trivial
skin, about 3.5χ wide, before reaching the topological phase. [click] The skin grows with the
same χ that pins the impostor, so it hides it. [click] If you see a zero-bias peak at the end
of a full shell, it is not a quasi-Majorana — although flux-tunable Andreev states and other
mechanisms still have to be excluded. If you don't see one, the skin may be hiding a true
MZM: sharp barriers are the way to go. Thank you.
:::

(0:40) Two checks. With short-range disorder below the minigap (paper Fig. 3), true MZM

## Why the transition is inverted in flux

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
- Partial shell: $V_\mathrm{Z}$ grows with $B$: trivial, then topological above $V_\mathrm{Z}^\mathrm{c}$
- Full shell, $m_J = 0$: a Majorana nanowire whose Zeeman energy is mostly **orbital**

::: {.eq}
$$
V_\mathrm{Z}^\mathrm{eff} = V_\mathrm{Z} + \frac{\tilde\phi}{2}\Bigl(\omega_R + \frac{\alpha}{R_\mathrm{av}}\Bigr), \qquad \tilde\phi = n - \frac{R_\mathrm{av}^2}{R_\mathrm{LP}^2}\frac{\Phi}{\Phi_0}
$$
:::

- Topological if $V_\mathrm{Z}^\mathrm{eff} > \sqrt{\Gamma_S^2 + \tilde\mu_0^2}$. Within a lobe $V_\mathrm{Z}^\mathrm{eff}$ **falls** with $\Phi$: MZM at low flux, quasi-MZM at high flux
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.stack}
![](assets/figs/s10b_inv_partial.svg)
![](assets/figs/s10b_inv_full.svg)
:::
:::
::::

::: {.refs}
S. Vaitiekėnas *et al.* Science **367**, eaav3392 (2020) · **C. Payá** *et al.* PRB **109**, 115428 (2024)
:::

## Models and parameters

| | Partial shell (1D, Suppl. S-I) | Full shell (Suppl. S-II) |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Common | $m^* = 0.023\,m_e$, $\Delta_0 = 0.23$ meV | $m^* = 0.023\,m_e$, $\Delta_0 = 0.23$ meV |
| Filling, SOC | $\mu_\mathrm{bulk} = 2$ meV, $\alpha = 40$ meV nm | $\mu_\mathrm{bulk} = 22.8$ meV, $\Delta U = 60$ meV, $\langle\alpha\rangle = 7$ meV nm |
| Coupling | $\Gamma_\mathrm{NS} = 3\Delta_0$, $V_C = 2V_\mathrm{Z}^\mathrm{c}$ | $\Gamma_\mathrm{NS} = 40\Delta_0$, $g = 10$ |
| Geometry | — | $R = 70$ nm, $d = 10$ nm, $\xi_d = 70$ nm |
| Smoothness (Fig. 1) | $\chi = 200$ nm | $\chi = 1$ µm |
| Disorder (Fig. 3) | $A_\mathrm{imp}/\sqrt{N} = 0.32\Delta_0$ | $A_\mathrm{imp}/\sqrt{N} = 0.02\Delta_0$ |

[Full shell: solid InAs-like core with a dome-shaped potential $U(r)$, radial Rashba SOC, flux and Zeeman; the Al shell is integrated out into a Little–Parks (Abrikosov–Gor'kov) self-energy; solved per $m_J$ sector.]{.small .ink2}

::: {.refs}
**C. Payá** *et al.* PRL **137**, 096606 (2026)
:::

## Electrostatics and skin widths

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
Projected on the $m_J = 0$, $m_r = 1$ mode that turns topological:

::: {.eq}
$$
\mu(z) \simeq \mu_\mathrm{bulk}\bigl(1 - 0.85\, e^{-z/\chi}\bigr)
$$
:::

| Case | Local phases along the wire |
|:--|:--|
| Partial, $V_\mathrm{Z}^{(2)}$ | topological for $z < 1.86\chi$, trivial beyond |
| Full, $\Phi^{(1)}$ | skin for $z < 3.42\chi$, then topological |
| Full, $\Phi^{(2)}$ | skin for $z < 3.50\chi$, topological up to $7.01\chi$ |

[Full-shell end signal below 1 % of its maximum for $\chi > 19$ nm (MZM and quasi-MZM)]{.small .ink2}

## Reproduce it: the partial-shell wire in Quantica.jl

```{.julia code-line-numbers="|3-4|6-8|10-12|14-15"}
lat = LP.square(; a0) |> supercell((1, 0))         # 1D chain, a0 = 5 nm

p2 = @onsite((r; μ = μ) -> σ0τz * (2t - μ)) +       # kinetic energy
     hopping((r, dr) -> -t * σ0τz, range = a0)

rashba = @hopping((r, dr; α = α) ->                  # Rashba SOC
     α * im * dr[1] / (2a0^2) * σyτz, range = a0)
zeeman = @onsite((; B = B) -> σzτ0 * B)              # Zeeman

hSM = lat |> hamiltonian(p2 + rashba + zeeman; orbitals = Val(4))
Σ! = @onsite!((o; ω = 0, B = B) -> o + τΓ * ΣSC(Δ0 * Δf(B; Bc), ω))
hSC = hSM |> Σ!                                      # proximity self-energy

h, L = build_barrier(hSC, pw, χ)                     # smooth end, μ(z)
g = h |> attach(gSC; region = r -> r[1] == L) |> greenfunction()
```

[`src/builders/apartial.jl` and `barrier.jl` in the paper's repository; the full shell uses `FullShell.build_cyl`]{.small .muted}
